title: Understand the structure and functions of a plant

lessons.title: The parts of a plant and what they do
lessons.html:
Knowing the plant helps you grow it

Every crop on the farm, from maize and cabbages to citrus trees and pasture grass, is a living plant. When you know what each part of the plant does, you understand why we water, fertilise, prune, weed and protect crops the way we do.

Roots

  • Hold the plant firmly in the soil.
  • Take up water and dissolved nutrients from the soil, mostly through tiny root hairs near the root tips.
  • Some roots store food, for example carrots, sweet potatoes and beetroot.

Roots need air as well as water. Waterlogged or very compacted soil can damage roots, which is why drainage and avoiding driving on wet lands matters.

Stem

  • Holds up the leaves, flowers and fruit towards the light.
  • Carries water and nutrients up from the roots in tubes called xylem.
  • Carries sugars made in the leaves to other parts in tubes called phloem.
  • Some stems store food, such as potato tubers and sugar cane.

Damage to the stem, for example ring-barking by animals or careless use of a brushcutter, cuts these transport tubes and can kill the plant.

Leaves

  • Make food for the plant through photosynthesis.
  • Release water vapour through small pores called stomata. This is called transpiration and it pulls water up from the roots.

Flowers, fruit and seeds

  • Flowers are for reproduction. Pollen from the male part (stamen) must reach the female part (pistil). Bees, wind and other insects help with pollination.
  • After pollination, the fruit develops and protects the seeds.
  • Seeds carry the next generation and contain stored food for the young plant.
PartMain job
RootAnchor, take up water and nutrients
StemSupport and transport
LeafMake food, transpiration
FlowerReproduction

lessons.title: How a plant lives and grows
lessons.html:
Photosynthesis: the plant's kitchen

In the leaves, the green substance chlorophyll captures energy from sunlight. The plant uses this energy to combine carbon dioxide from the air with water from the soil to make sugar. Oxygen is released into the air.

Carbon dioxide + water + sunlight energy = sugar + oxygen

The sugar is the plant's food. It is used for energy and to build stems, roots, fruit and seeds. Anything that reduces leaf area or light, such as pests eating leaves, disease, weeds shading crops or plants planted too close together, reduces the food the plant can make and so reduces yield.

Respiration

Like animals, plants use oxygen to break down sugar and release energy. This happens day and night in all living cells, including roots. This is another reason roots need air in the soil.

What a plant needs to grow

  • Light – for photosynthesis.
  • Water – for photosynthesis, transport and to keep cells firm. A plant without enough water wilts.
  • Air – carbon dioxide for leaves, oxygen for roots.
  • Nutrients – nitrogen for leafy growth, phosphorus for roots and flowering, potassium for fruit quality and strength, plus smaller amounts of others.
  • Suitable temperature – each crop has a range. Frost kills many tender crops like tomatoes and bananas.

Growth stages

  1. Germination – the seed takes up water, swells and sends out a root and shoot.
  2. Vegetative growth – the plant grows leaves, stems and roots.
  3. Flowering – the plant produces flowers.
  4. Fruit and seed development – fruit fills and ripens.
  5. Maturity – the crop is ready to harvest.

Farm work is timed to these stages. For example, maize needs enough water at tasselling and silking, and weeding is most important while young plants are small.

Key points

  • Roots anchor and take up water and nutrients; they also need air.
  • Stems support the plant and transport water (xylem) and sugars (phloem).
  • Leaves make food through photosynthesis using light, water and carbon dioxide.
  • Flowers produce fruit and seeds after pollination.
  • Plants need light, water, air, nutrients and the right temperature.
